title: handshake-fragmentation-probe-notes
content:
Summary:

This note captures a small-bench exploration into handshake fragmentation — the runtime and $$ impact when network/codec/TLS/session-warmup operations for short-turn conversational requests are split across separate RPCs versus when they are fused into a single admission. The angle: tiny-turn, high-cardinality chat workloads (mobile assistants, microinteractions) show disproportionate p95 penalties when handshake steps are repeated or badly fragmented. We wanted a compact, actionable profile we can use as collateral (team brief + quickcharts) and a short experiment plan to validate product knobs (keepalive, session-reuse, lazy-decode prewarm).

Background / motivation:
- Observed in telemetry: p50 remains fine, but p95/p99 spikes on mobile-origin short requests (median tokens < 20).
- Hypothesis: repeated handshake fragments (TCP/TLS + request-level auth + decoder prewarm) incur a stacking of micro-latencies. When any step is non-aggregated across client flows, tail multiplies.
- Business tradeoff: fragmentation sometimes reduces resource holding time (good for throughput), but increases tail latency and therefore SLO violations and perceived UX regressions.

What we measured (local small-cluster synthetic):
- Workloads: tiny-turn chat (mean tokens=12), medium-turn (mean tokens=80).
- Two server setups: FRAGMENT (default: separate admission for connection, auth token fetch, model prewarm), POOL (fused admission with fast-path reuse + session cache).
- Key metrics: p50, p95, p99 in ms; cost proxy = USD-per-1k-requests (simple amortized GPU-time + 10% infra premium).

ASCII summary table (averages over 10k requests each):

Scenario                       | p50 ms | p95 ms | p99 ms | est $/1k reqs | notes
-------------------------------|--------|--------|--------|---------------|-------------------------------
Tiny-turn FRAGMENT             |   38   |  312   |  620   |   4.5         | repeated prewarm + auth roundtrips
Tiny-turn POOL                 |   36   |  86    |  140   |   4.9         | slightly higher amortized $ due to idle slots, much lower tail
Medium-turn FRAGMENT           |  92    |  130   |  200   |   9.8         | handshake overhead amortized by tokens
Medium-turn POOL               |  90    |  118   |  160   | 10.1          | similar dollars, slightly better tail

Interpretation:
- Tail wins for POOL in tiny-turns: p95 drops ~72% and p99 drops ~77%. The cost proxy rises modestly (~9%) because pooled slots keep some capacity warm; however, realized UX from p95->p99 reduction is large.
- In medium-turn workloads the delta shrinks because the handshake cost is amortized across more token decode time.
- The qualitative tradeoff: pool reduces tail at small extra cost; fragment reduces idle burn but amplifies tails.

Text sparklines (approx):
- Tiny-turn FRAGMENT p95: ▅▂▁▁▁▁▙▇▇▇ (long right tail bursts)
- Tiny-turn POOL p95: ▅▅▅▅▅▅▅▅▇▁ (tight distribution)

Micrograph: latency composition (avg p95 slice):
- FRAGMENT tiny-turn: TCP handshake 10ms | TLS 28ms | auth fetch 45ms | decoder prewarm 110ms | decode 120ms | queue jitter  - temporal sum = 313ms (matches observed)
- POOL tiny-turn: reuse path -> TCP/TLS negligible (5ms) | auth cached 5ms | decoder warmed 22ms | decode 120ms | queue jitter = 86ms

Operational knobs to explore (prioritized):
1) Session reuse TTL tuning (client keepalive + server session cache).
   - Quick test: TTL=30s vs TTL=300s. Expect: p95 delta biggest at 300s, cost rises with idle retention.
2) Lazy decoder prewarm: start prewarm during auth exchange (overlap) instead of after auth success.
3) Admission fusion for microrequests: short path that checks auth token but does not allocate full reserved slot.
4) Short-slot pooling: keep N micro-slots with limited KV cache; cheaper than full slot but fast warmup.

Simple decision heuristics for product collateral (one-pager):
- If median tokens < 30 and >60% requests are single-turn < 15 tokens: recommend enabling "micro-slotpool" + session reuse TTL=120s and lazy prewarm.
- For long-tail conversational workloads (50+ tokens): default pooling optional; optimize for throughput.

Risk and open questions:
- Security: longer session reuse interacts with token revocation windows. Need to coordinate with auth team for a session revocation mechanism.
- Cost accounting: our simple $/1k proxy ignores memory reslice costs for many tiny slots; engineering to produce a more accurate amortization model.
- Telemetry fidelity: need to add tags for "handshake-phase durations" into trace spans (TCP/TLS/auth/prewarm/decode) to validate across customers.

Experiment plan (short):
- Phase 0 (1 week): synthetic benchmark matrix for TTLs [30s, 120s, 300s], pool sizes [0, 8, 32], lazy-prewarm on/off. Collect p50/p95/p99, CPU/GPU duty, mem footprint.
- Phase 1 (2 weeks): Canary on low-volume tenants with mobile-heavy mix. Add tracing spans for handshake phases.
- Phase 2 (2 weeks): Rollout with telemetry dashboard + alert for p95 regression; measure revenue-adjacent metrics (SLA violations, support tickets).

Collateral visuals to produce for stakeholder deck (text-first):
- Waterfall bar per scenario showing composition of p95 (authoritative for PG).
- Cost vs p95 scatter with shading for token-length buckets.
- Small table comparing UX-weighted score (0-100) where p95 drives 80% weight for mobile microinteractions.

Action items and owners:
- Add handshake-phase spans to tracer (backend-infra) -> Owner: Rafael Gomez -> due: 2029-03-18
- Run Phase 0 matrix and upload CSV -> Owner: Priya Desai -> due: 2029-03-15
- Draft one-pager for product marketing (include simple recommendation heuristics) -> Owner: Maya Thompson -> due: 2029-03-20

Notes to self / rough math:
- If pooled micro-slots cost +9% dollars but reduce p95 p99 for tiny-turns by 70%, expected UA retention uplift could be modelled; trivial sensitivity: 1% retention improvement on a 100k DAU mobile cohort -> large long-term revenue impact; product should weigh against infra operating margin.

Questions for review:
- Are we comfortable with a 120s TTL as default for micro-slotpool? (security team input needed)
- Should we treat micro-slotpool as an opt-in feature per customer or expose as a server-side heuristic?

End of probe notes.
